questions.stem: A worker standing on the ground at \(A\) observes that the angle of elevation to a hot-air balloon hovering 100 m above the ground to be \(41^\circ\). The balloon remains attached to the ground at point \(A\) by a long rope. Find the length of the rope to the nearest metre.
questions.hint: Draw a right-angled triangle. The height is the opposite side and the rope is the hypotenuse.

Use the sine ratio: \(\sin(\theta) = \frac{\text{Opposite}}{\text{Hypotenuse}}\)
Rearrange to solve for \(x\).

questions.stem:
A plane flies 800 km north from the airport and then 1250 km west.

Find the bearing, to the nearest degree, of the airport from the plane at the end of its flight.
questions.hint: Draw a diagram. Finding the bearing from the plane means starting at the plane, facing North, and turning clockwise until you face the airport.

steps.explain: Draw a diagram of the flight path. Let the plane be at the top left of a right-angled triangle.
Find the angle \(\theta\) inside the triangle at the plane's position. The opposite side is 800 km and the adjacent side is 1250 km.
Calculate \(\theta\).
The bearing is measured clockwise from North. From North to East is \(90^\circ\). The angle to the airport is \(90^\circ + \theta\).
Round to the nearest degree.

questions.hint: Use Pythagoras' theorem: \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2\).

Calculate the squares.

questions.stem: An engineer erects a vertical radio mast on horizontal ground at \(O\). Three wires from point \(A\) are fixed to the mast at points \(X\), \(Y\) and \(Z\). The wires form straight lines and \(XY=YZ\). (i) Prove that \(OY=\dfrac12(OX+OZ)\). (ii) Hence prove that \(\tan(\angle XAO)+\tan(\angle ZAO)=2\tan(\angle YAO)\).
questions.hint: For (i), X, Y, Z are points on a vertical line, so use basic 1D distance properties. For (ii), use right-angled triangles AOX, AOY, AOZ to write the tangent ratios.
questions.solution: (i) \(OY = \frac{1}{2}(OX+OZ)\) since \(Y\) is the midpoint of \(XZ\). (ii) Divide the result of (i) by \(OA\) to get \(\tan(\angle YAO) = \frac{1}{2}(\tan(\angle XAO) + \tan(\angle ZAO))\).

steps.explain: The points \(O\), \(X\), \(Y\), and \(Z\) all lie on the vertical mast. Since the distances between the fixing points are equal (\(XY=YZ\)), \(Y\) is the midpoint of the segment \(XZ\).
steps.work: \(OY - OX = OZ - OY \Rightarrow 2\cdot OY = OX + OZ \Rightarrow OY = \dfrac{1}{2}(OX+OZ)\)

steps.explain: In the right-angled triangles \(\triangle AOX\), \(\triangle AOY\), and \(\triangle AOZ\), the angle at \(O\) is \(90°\). We can write the tangent of each angle at \(A\) as Opposite/Adjacent.
Add the tangents for \(\angle XAO\) and \(\angle ZAO\).
Substitute the identity from part (i) where \(OX+OZ = 2\cdot OY\).
Rewrite the right-hand side using the tangent ratio for \(Y\).

questions.stem:

A right triangle has hypotenuse \(24\text{ cm}\), adjacent side \(16\text{ cm}\) (both meeting at the angle \(x°\)).
questions.hint: The 16 cm side is adjacent to \(x°\), and 24 cm is the hypotenuse — use \(\cos\).

steps.explain: Use the cosine ratio, since 16 cm is adjacent to \(x°\) and 24 cm is the hypotenuse.
Solve for \(x\) using the inverse cosine.
Evaluate and round to the nearest whole number.

questions.stem: In a right triangle with hypotenuse 12 and \(\sin\theta=\dfrac14\) (\(\theta\) at the top vertex), find the exact value of \(\cos\theta\), without using a calculator.
questions.hint: Since \(\sin\theta=\tfrac14=\tfrac{c}{12}\), find the opposite side \(c\) first, then use Pythagoras to find the adjacent side, then form \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}\).

steps.explain: Since \(\sin\theta=\dfrac14\) and the hypotenuse is 12, find the side opposite \(\theta\) (call it \(c\)).
Use Pythagoras' theorem to find the remaining side (adjacent to \(\theta\)), call it \(a\).
Form \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac{a}{12}\).
Simplify the fraction.

questions.stem: By considering a right-angled triangle, explain why \(\sin\theta\) can never equal \(\dfrac95\).

steps.explain: In a right-angled triangle, \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}\), where the hypotenuse is always the LONGEST side of the triangle (it is opposite the right angle, the largest angle).
Since the opposite side can never be longer than the hypotenuse, the ratio \(\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}\) can never exceed 1.
Since \(\dfrac95=1.8>1\), this value is impossible for \(\sin\theta\) to take.

questions.stem: A pyramid \(VABCD\) has a square base of side length 8 cm. \(M\) is the midpoint of diagonal \(AC\), and \(VM\) (the perpendicular height) is 10 cm. Calculate the size of \(\angle VAM\), correct to the nearest degree.
questions.hint: First find the diagonal \(AC\) using Pythagoras (\(AC=\sqrt{8^2+8^2}\)), then \(AM=\tfrac12AC\). In right-angled \(\triangle VAM\) (right angle at \(M\)), use \(\tan\angle VAM=\dfrac{VM}{AM}\).

steps.explain: Find the diagonal \(AC\) of the square base using Pythagoras' theorem.
\(M\) is the midpoint of \(AC\), so \(AM=\tfrac12AC\).
In right-angled \(\triangle VAM\) (right angle at \(M\), since \(VM\) is the perpendicular height), use the tangent ratio with \(VM\) opposite \(\angle VAM\) and \(AM\) adjacent.
Solve using the inverse tangent and round to the nearest degree.

questions.stem: A submarine dives from the ocean surface at an angle of \(22°\). It travels a diagonal distance of 650 metres before reaching the bottom. Find the depth of the ocean, correct to the nearest whole number.
questions.hint: The depth is the side OPPOSITE the \(22°\) angle, and 650 m is the hypotenuse (diagonal path) — use \(\sin\).

steps.explain: The depth (vertical drop) is opposite the \(22°\) angle of descent, and 650 m (the diagonal path) is the hypotenuse. Use the sine ratio.
Solve for \(d\).
Evaluate and round to the nearest whole number.

questions.stem: A large flagpole \(AB\) stands on top of a building. From \(D\), located \(50\) metres from \(C\), the angle of elevation to the top of the building is \(45°\). The angle of elevation from \(D\) to the top of the flagpole is \(48°\). Let \(b\) be the height of the building, and \(f\) be the length of the flagpole. Find the height of the flagpole, correct to the nearest metre.
questions.hint: First find \(b\) using \(\tan45°=\dfrac{b}{50}\). Then find \(f+b\) using \(\tan48°=\dfrac{f+b}{50}\), and subtract.

steps.explain: In the smaller right triangle \(DCB\), use the \(45°\) angle of elevation to find the building height \(b\).
In the larger right triangle \(DCA\), use the \(48°\) angle of elevation to find the combined height \(f+b\).
Subtract the building height \(b\) from the combined height to isolate the flagpole length \(f\).
Round to the nearest metre.

questions.hint: \(FH\) is adjacent to \(\angle BHF\), and \(BH\) is the hypotenuse of right triangle \(BFH\) — use \(\cos\).

steps.explain: In right triangle \(BFH\) (right angle at \(F\), since \(BF\) is a vertical edge of the prism), \(FH\) is adjacent to \(\angle BHF\) and \(BH\) is the hypotenuse.
Rearrange to solve for \(BH\).
Evaluate.

questions.hint: \(x=CB\) is opposite \(\angle A\), and \(AB=20\) is the hypotenuse — use \(\sin\).

steps.explain: Relative to \(\angle A\), \(x=CB\) is the opposite side and \(AB=20\) is the hypotenuse, so use the sine ratio.
Multiply both sides by \(20\) to solve for \(x\).
Evaluate and round to one decimal place.

questions.stem: Point \(A\) is shown on a diagram, at \(28°\) measured from due South, on the South-East side. (a) What is the compass bearing of point \(A\) from \(O\)? (b) Find the true bearing of \(O\) from \(A\).

parts.stem: (a) What is the compass bearing of point \(A\) from \(O\)?
parts.hint: Compass bearings are measured from North or South, toward East or West, whichever is closer. Since \(A\) is closer to the South line here, measure the angle FROM South.

steps.explain: The angle shown, \(28°\), is measured from the EAST line toward point \(A\) — but for a compass bearing, we need the angle from the nearer of North/South. Since \(A\) is much closer to the South direction, find the angle from South.
Point \(A\) is in the South-East quadrant, so the compass bearing is expressed as South, this angle, East.

parts.stem: (b) Find the true bearing of \(O\) from \(A\).
parts.hint: The bearing of \(O\) from \(A\) is the REVERSE of the bearing of \(A\) from \(O\) — add or subtract \(180°\) from the bearing of \(A\) from \(O\).

steps.explain: First find the true bearing of \(A\) from \(O\) (measured clockwise from North). Since \(A\) is S62°E, this true bearing is \(180°-62°=118°\).
The bearing of \(O\) from \(A\) (looking back) is this bearing plus \(180°\) (since it is less than \(180°\)).

questions.stem: Allen and Ben were camping at site \(P\). Allen walked on a bearing of \(035°\text{T}\) for 7 km to location \(A\). Ben walked on a bearing of \(125°\text{T}\) for 9 km to location \(B\).

parts.stem: (a) What is the size of \(\angle APB\)?
parts.hint: \(\angle APB\) is the difference between the two bearings measured from \(P\) (both measured clockwise from North).

steps.explain: The angle \(\angle APB\) between the two paths from \(P\) is the difference between their bearings.

parts.stem: (b) Find the true bearing of location \(B\) from location \(A\), correct to the nearest degree.
parts.hint: First find \(\angle PAB\) using \(\tan\angle PAB=\dfrac{9}{7}\) (right-angled triangle \(APB\)). Then use the fact that the bearing from \(A\) back to \(P\) is \(215°\text{T}\) (i.e. \(35°+180°\)), and subtract \(\angle PAB\) appropriately.

steps.explain: Since \(\triangle APB\) is right-angled at \(P\) (from part a), use the tangent ratio to find \(\angle PAB\), with \(PB=9\) opposite and \(PA=7\) adjacent.

Find \(\angle PAC\), where \(C\) represents North at \(A\): since the bearing of \(A\) from \(P\) is \(035°\text{T}\), by alternate angles (North lines at \(P\) and \(A\) are parallel), \(\angle NAP=35°\) (the angle between North at \(A\) and line \(AP\)).
Find \(\angle BAC\) (i.e. \(\angle NAB\) minus \(\angle NAP\)), which requires subtracting: \(\angle BAP-\angle NAP\).

The bearing of \(P\) from \(A\) is \(215°\text{T}\) (reverse of \(035°\)). The bearing of \(B\) from \(A\) is found by subtracting \(\angle BAC\) from \(180°\) (accounting for the direction \(B\) lies relative to line \(AP\)), following the geometry of the figure.
Round to the nearest degree.

questions.stem: Town \(A\) is \(2.6\text{ km}\) east of Town \(C\). Town \(C\) is \(1.7\text{ km}\) due south of Town \(B\). Find the bearing of Town \(B\) from Town \(A\), correct to the nearest degree.
questions.hint: From \(A\), the direction to \(C\) is due west (\(270°\text{T}\)). Find the angle \(\angle CAB=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1.7}{2.6}\right)\), then add it to \(270°\) since \(B\) is tilted from west toward north.

steps.explain: In right triangle \(ACB\) (right angle at \(C\)), find the angle \(\angle CAB\) using the tangent ratio.
From \(A\), Town \(C\) lies due west, i.e. on a bearing of \(270°\text{T}\). Since \(B\) is north of \(C\), the direction to \(B\) is rotated \(33.2°\) further around (toward north) from due west.
Evaluate and round to the nearest degree.

questions.stem: A plane flies from Melbourne at a bearing of \(310^\circ\). After flying 600km it is at a point P.

parts.stem: How far North of Melbourne is the plane when it reaches Point P (nearest km)?

steps.explain: A bearing of \(310^\circ\) means the plane flies North-West. The angle between North (\(360^\circ\)) and the flight path is \(360^\circ - 310^\circ = 50^\circ\), shown below.

parts.stem: What is the bearing of Melbourne from point P?

steps.explain: The bearing of P from Melbourne is \(310^\circ\). To find the return bearing (Melbourne from P), we add or subtract \(180^\circ\) depending on whether the original bearing is greater or less than \(180^\circ\). The diagram below shows the return bearing measured at P.

questions.stem: The distance of a ski slope is 415m with a vertical drop of 115m. Find the angle of depression from the top of the slope to the nearest degree.

steps.explain: Draw the situation. The skier starts at point A (top of slope), descends to point B (bottom). The slope AB = 415 m is the **hypotenuse**. The vertical drop BC = 115 m is the side **opposite** to angle θ. The angle of depression θ is measured from the **horizontal** at A downward to the slope.

Identify which sides are known relative to the angle of depression θ at A. The **opposite** side (vertical drop) = 115 m and the **hypotenuse** (slope distance) = 415 m are highlighted. This tells us to use the **sin** ratio.
Calculate the angle using the inverse sine function.

questions.stem: An observer on top of a building 66m high, finds the angle of elevation to the top of a taller building to be \\(34^\circ\\). The angle of depression to the foot of the same building is \\(51^\circ\\). Calculate the height of the taller building, given the buildings are on the same ground level, to the nearest metre.

steps.explain: Let \\(d\\) be the horizontal distance between the buildings. Use the lower triangle (angle of depression) to find \\(d\\).
Let \\(h\\) be the height of the taller building above the observer. Use the upper triangle (angle of elevation) to find \\(h\\).
Calculate the total height of the taller building.

questions.stem: A light plane takes off flying due north, then turns and flies due west. The plane then has a bearing of \\(340^\circ\\) from its starting point with a direct distance of 16km. Calculate the due north distance that the plane flew, to the nearest km.

steps.explain: A bearing of \\(340^\circ\\) means the plane is \\(360^\circ - 340^\circ = 20^\circ\\) West of North from the starting point.
Form a right-angled triangle. The hypotenuse is the direct distance (16km), and the due north distance is the adjacent side to the \\(20^\circ\\) angle.
Calculate the due north distance.

questions.stem: On a golf course, the tree is a distance of 130m due west from the pin (the flag stick). Bruce’s first shot hits the ball 100m but not at the correct angle. On his second shot, Bruce hits the ball 35m and gets it in the hole. Find the bearing that he hits his first stroke (to the nearest degree).

steps.explain: The path forms a triangle with sides 130m, 100m, and 35m. We want to find the angle \\(a\\) at the tree.
Use the Cosine Rule to find \\(a\\).
Calculate the value.
Find the angle \\(a\\).
The bearing is measured clockwise from North. Since the pin is due East (\\(090^\circ\\)), and the angle \\(a\\) is North of East, subtract \\(9^\circ\\) from \\(090^\circ\\).
